content: I just opened cslib#468, which I'm aware is still ugly. (This is after many hours of cleanup, after the functioning proofs, already!) It defines basic "growth rates", in particular several important ones that aren't a big-O or little-O, gives several equivalent definitions, lots of their closure properties and composition properties, and establishes their ordering.

I'm hopeful that for things like time or space complexity classes, this can be used as the standard spelling for certain classes of functions. It's what I've used at CircuitComp (which I do eventually want to just entirely merge into CSLib and then kill) for defining circuit complexity classes
You might want to make the exponents explicit in all classes. In the exponential classes one also needs to make the base explicit.
I'm confused. Of course you can do that, but that's exactly what IsBigO already is for. The point is that often we want to talk about the case where the exponent isn't explicit.
I would appreciate some eyes / opinion on cslib#468 ! It's my first step to merging in stuff from CircuitComp which I would like to eventually have live entirely in CSLib.
I think it’s failing CI right now
I am more than happy to review (and assigned myself) but the +3500 gave me a bit of pause. I'll probably suggest splitting off a few hundred lines or so once I do a first high-level pass.
Yes, I fully expect that I will need to split it, and probably clean up more too. This isn't merge ready! :) I was rather seeking initial feedback before embarking on that
It’s still failing CI. I think it just needs a run of lake exe mk_all —module
If you look at the CI messages, you'll see it's the environment linters. I'd say these can wait until we're at the point of splitting things up.
I actually don't understand the topNamespace linter. It complains that "Primrec.factorial is not namespaced". But, Primrec is exactly the right namespace for this.
There might be a bug in that linter, I've seen it occasionally behave oddly since moving to the module system. (This is a CSLib-specific one I wrote)

Okay, think I fixed the lints now. :)

I'm still curious to hear how welcome some library like this is. It should be split up into multiple files certainly but I wanted to hear if anyone had ideas for how exactly.

I would appreciate some examples of how to apply this growth rate to a concrete algorithmic bound to help me digest the PR. For example, in cslib merge sort, there is an upper bound of n log n, which is not expressed as GrowthRate.linearithmic. Can you show how to convert that to GrowthRate.linearithmic?

In light of the 3k-line PR, can you share a roadmap for it? I prefer to review a small component at a time. We can start with a minimal working version so that it can state the time complexity of merge sort asymptotically? Then, we can adding more lemmas later on for completeness.

I split it into several files, which I think makes the roadmap a bit clearer. GrowthRate/Defs.lean gives the basic operations to coarsely add, multiply, or exponentiate classes. So then (in Closure.lean) we have equalities like GrowthRate.poly = GrowthRate.linear ^ GrowthRate.const or GrowthRate.poly * GrowthRate.poly = GrowthRate.poly.

For the example of the mergesort, so what's currently in MergeSort.lean is that
(mergeSort xs).time ≤ n * clog 2 n. In my PR, I already have:

  • theorem clog_mem_log2 : Nat.clog 2 ∈ log
  • theorem linearithmic_of_linear_mul (hf : f ∈ linear) (hg : g ∈ log) : f * g ∈ linearithmic
  • theorem mono (hf : f ∈ S) (hg : g ≤ f) : g ∈ S
    So then it's pretty immediate: if you want to show that mergeSort's time is ∈ linearithmic, then you apply GrowthRate.mono to reduce it to showing that n * clog 2 n ∈ linearithmic. Then apply linearithmic_of_linear_mul . The first argument is the trivial id ∈ linear, the second is clog_mem_log2 .
    So it's pretty quick, like three lines

A big part of the reason I want this is so that we can reasonably express things like "I had a linearithmic function, if I add some constants and linear functions, that doensn't affect it" and then "Now I raise it a constant power, it's still in poly". And what do I mean by "poly?" that can be nat powers, real number powers, sometimes you want A * (B * n) ^ C, sometimes you want (A + B * n) ^ C. Same thing for logs, sometimes you want Nat.log, sometimes Nat.log2, sometimes Nat.clog, sometimes Real.log, sometimes Real.logb ... it's nice to have one API that can convert between this mostly painlessly.
